143.text:
Documentaries about nature, history and social problems attract millions of viewers on television and streaming platforms, and this essay will discuss the role of documentaries in educating the public, focusing on how they present evidence and how they raise awareness.

To begin with, documentaries educate the public by showing real events and complex issues in an accessible way. Film combines evidence, interviews and images that make topics such as climate or history memorable. A viewer who watches a documentary about plastic in the oceans, for example, sees turtles caught in nets and beaches covered in rubbish, which is far more powerful than reading a statistic. Experts explain difficult ideas in plain language, and animation, maps and archive footage make them easier to grasp. People who would never open a scientific textbook may therefore learn about medicine, space or economics in an evening.

Furthermore, documentaries raise awareness and encourage action. They bring attention to problems that are neglected in the news, such as modern slavery, and they can change opinions and policies. Several films about food production have led consumers to change their habits and governments to tighten rules. Schools use documentaries to bring lessons to life, and they allow viewers to visit places and cultures they could never see. However, directors may present a one-sided view or simplify, and viewers should not accept every claim without question. Documentaries are best treated as a starting point for further reading, discussion and independent thinking.

In conclusion, documentaries play an important role in educating the public by presenting evidence vividly and drawing attention to important issues, provided that viewers remain critical.

Giáo dục bằng sự kiện thật, vấn đề phức tạp dễ tiếp cận: phim kết hợp bằng chứng, phỏng vấn, hình ảnh; ví dụ người xem phim rác nhựa ở đại dương thấy rùa mắc lưới, bãi biển đầy rác mạnh hơn thống kê; chuyên gia giải thích dễ hiểu, hoạt hình, bản đồ, tư liệu; người không đọc giáo trình học y học, vũ trụ, kinh tế.

Nâng nhận thức, khuyến khích hành động: chú ý vấn đề bị bỏ quên (nô lệ hiện đại), thay đổi ý kiến, chính sách; phim về thực phẩm đổi thói quen, siết quy định; trường dùng; thăm nơi, văn hoá; nhưng thiên lệch, đơn giản hoá, điểm khởi đầu.
Vai trò quan trọng nếu người xem phê phán.

144.text:
Many people now watch new films on a laptop or television a few weeks after release, and many feel that streaming services have reduced box office sales. I agree to a large extent, since streaming has reduced cinema attendance for ordinary films, although big releases still fill theatres.

To begin with, streaming has reduced cinema attendance for ordinary films. Viewers can watch a wide choice at home for a monthly fee. A family of four who would pay a large sum for tickets, snacks and parking, for example, can instead watch several films at home for a fraction of the cost, and they can pause, rewind and choose the time. Studios that launch their own platforms sometimes release films online on the same day as in cinemas, which gives people little reason to go out. Medium-budget dramas and comedies, which once earned steady revenue, have suffered most, and many small cinemas have closed.

However, the large screen, sound and shared atmosphere of cinemas keep attracting audiences to major films. Spectacular action films, superhero stories and animated features regularly earn record sums, because many people want an experience that a home cannot match. A group of friends who see a new blockbuster together, for example, enjoy the excitement of reacting with a crowd. Other factors have also reduced sales, including rising ticket prices, the pandemic and competition from games and social media, so streaming is not the only cause. Cinemas can respond by offering comfortable seats, special screenings and events, which makes a visit more than just watching a film.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that streaming has reduced box office sales, particularly for modest films, but cinemas will survive by offering experiences that homes cannot.

154.text:
Programmes in which strangers share a house or compete for a prize are popular around the world, and many people think that reality television encourages bad behaviour. I agree to a large extent, since such shows often reward conflict and shallow fame, although a few have positive aspects.

To begin with, reality television often rewards conflict and shallow fame, which can encourage poor behaviour. Producers choose arguments, insults and scandals that attract viewers, so young audiences may imitate rudeness and think fame matters more than effort. A contestant who shouts at others and receives millions of views, for example, may become a celebrity, which sends the message that aggression is a path to success. Editing creates villains and exaggerates quarrels, and participants are encouraged to gossip, lie and betray each other in order to win. Viewers who watch such behaviour week after week may come to see it as normal and may copy the language and attitudes in their own schools and offices.

However, not all reality shows are harmful, and a few teach skills or kindness. Cooking and singing competitions, for example, show contestants who practise for years and support each other, and home renovation programmes demonstrate practical skills. Some documentaries in the genre follow families through difficult times and increase understanding of other people. The influence therefore depends on the programme and on the viewer. Parents should talk with children about what they watch, and broadcasters should avoid deliberately provoking conflict or humiliating participants. Viewers need critical awareness and should remember that what they see has been edited for entertainment.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that reality television encourages bad behaviour, but its effect depends on the programme and on how critically it is watched.

164.text:
A shocking headline can be shared with thousands of people before anyone checks whether it is true, and many feel that fake news spreads too easily online. I agree with this view, since sharing is instant and emotional stories travel fastest, although some measures can limit the problem.

To begin with, fake news spreads too easily because sharing is instant and emotional stories travel fastest. Users forward posts without checking, algorithms promote shocking content, and false stories can reach millions before corrections appear. A false report about a medicine that cures a disease, for example, may be shared by worried relatives who believe they are helping, and some may then refuse proper treatment. Studies show that untrue stories are more likely to be shared than accurate ones because they are surprising and provoke anger or fear. Anyone can create a convincing website or video using cheap tools, and fake accounts can make a story look popular.

Furthermore, the consequences are serious. False claims about vaccines have reduced immunisation, rumours during elections influence voters and invented stories about minorities have caused violence. However, the situation is not hopeless. Verification tools, fact-checking organisations and labels on disputed posts help users to identify misleading content, and platforms can reduce the reach of repeated offenders. Media education is also vital: schools should teach students to check sources, look for evidence and think before sharing. When these steps are combined with fair laws against deliberate disinformation, fake news will find it harder to spread.

In conclusion, I agree that fake news spreads too easily online, and responsibility is shared by platforms, governments, schools and ordinary users.

Hậu quả nghiêm trọng: vắc-xin giảm tiêm chủng, bầu cử, bạo lực chống thiểu số; công cụ xác minh, tổ chức kiểm chứng, nhãn; nền tảng giảm tiếp cận; giáo dục truyền thông: kiểm nguồn, tìm bằng chứng, suy nghĩ trước khi chia sẻ; luật công bằng chống thông tin sai cố ý.

186.text:
Children watch cartoons and educational programmes for hours every week, and some people think that advertising should be banned from children's programmes. I agree to a large extent, since such a ban would protect young viewers, although the television industry will need alternative funding.

To begin with, advertising should be banned from children's programmes because it exploits young viewers. Children cannot judge persuasion, and adverts fuel pester power, which means that they keep demanding products from their parents. A child who sees a toy advertised between two cartoons, for example, believes that she needs it, and a parent who refuses may face tears and arguments. Many adverts promote sugary snacks and expensive items, which encourages unhealthy habits and materialism. Some countries, including Sweden and Norway, have banned or strictly limited advertising aimed at children, and they have not seen the quality of programmes decline. A programme that is free of commercial breaks allows children to concentrate on the story and the lesson.

However, channels rely on advertising income, so alternative funding is needed. If commercial channels lose income, they may reduce the quality or quantity of children's programmes, which would harm young viewers. Public funding, subsidies for educational content or limited sponsorship that does not promote products can fill the gap. In addition, children now watch many videos online, where a ban on television alone would have little effect, so rules should cover digital platforms too. Parents can also teach children how advertising works. Quality television for children can survive without ads, as public broadcasters have shown for decades.

In conclusion, I agree that advertising should be banned from children's programmes, provided that governments find other sources of funding.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: cấm quảng cáo trong chương trình trẻ em — largely agree

Quảng cáo khai thác người xem trẻ: trẻ không phán đoán được thuyết phục, thúc ép cha mẹ; ví dụ trẻ thấy đồ chơi giữa hai phim hoạt hình tin cần có, cha mẹ từ chối bị khóc, cãi; quảng cáo kẹo, đồ đắt khuyến khích thói quen xấu, vật chất; Thuỵ Điển, Na Uy cấm hoặc hạn chế mà chất lượng không giảm; chương trình không quảng cáo tập trung.

201.text:
Advertisements for crisps, soft drinks and fast food appear on billboards, in magazines and during popular television shows, and some people say that advertising for unhealthy foods should be restricted. I agree with this view, since such advertising shapes choices, especially those of children, and contributes to health problems.

To begin with, advertising for unhealthy foods should be restricted because it influences what people eat. Advertisers spend large sums to make sweets and fast food look exciting, and the constant exposure makes them seem normal parts of daily life. A teenager who sees a sports star drinking a sugary beverage in an advertisement, for example, may link it with success and energy. Obesity, diabetes and heart disease are increasing worldwide, and unhealthy diets are a major cause, which burdens hospitals and reduces productivity. Children are particularly vulnerable because they cannot recognise persuasion, and food preferences formed early often last for life. Limits on broadcasting times and on advertising near schools have helped to reduce the consumption of unhealthy products in some countries.

However, restrictions should be accompanied by other measures. Food companies argue that their products are legal and that individuals should decide for themselves, and a complete ban would reduce revenue for media and companies. A balanced approach would restrict the advertising of the unhealthiest products at times when children are watching, require clear nutritional information and encourage adverts for healthy alternatives. Education in schools can teach children about nutrition, and healthier food should be made affordable. Together, these steps lower the demand for junk food without removing freedom of choice.

In conclusion, I agree that advertising for unhealthy foods should be restricted, since it affects health, but restrictions should be part of a broader strategy.

214.text:
Streaming platforms release whole series at once, and many people watch ten episodes in a single weekend, so many people think that binge-watching TV has negative effects. I agree to a large extent when it is excessive, although occasional marathons are harmless.

To begin with, binge-watching harms health and time use when it is excessive. Hours of sitting reduce sleep and exercise and replace study or social time. A student who stays up until four in the morning to finish a series, for example, will be exhausted at lectures and may fall behind with her work. Long periods of inactivity are linked to weight gain, back pain and heart problems, and blue light from screens disturbs sleep. Researchers have also found that heavy bingers feel more lonely and more depressed than moderate viewers, partly because they may avoid friends and activities. Some people find it hard to stop, since autoplay starts the next episode automatically and the story is designed to be gripping.

However, binge-watching is not always harmful. Watching a favourite series with friends on a rainy weekend can relax and bond people, and shared programmes provide topics for conversation. Compared with stressful work, a few hours of entertainment can be a legitimate way to recover, and many programmes are educational or artistic. The effect therefore depends on moderation and planning. Viewers can set limits, turn off autoplay, take breaks to move around and avoid watching late at night before important duties. Parents can also guide children's viewing habits.

In conclusion, I agree that binge-watching has negative effects when excessive, but moderate viewing is harmless and can be enjoyable.

224.text:
Pop-up windows, videos that start automatically and adverts that seem to follow users from site to site are part of everyday browsing, and many feel that online advertising is intrusive. I agree with this view, since it interrupts and tracks users, although it pays for much free content.

To begin with, online advertising is intrusive because it interrupts and tracks users. Pop-ups, autoplay videos and personalised tracking disturb browsing and collect data. A reader who tries to follow a news article, for example, may have to close three banners, wait for an advert to end and then find that the page jumps while it loads. Companies collect information about searches, locations and purchases to target adverts, which many people find uncomfortable, especially when they see ads for something that they mentioned in a private conversation. Mobile phone users also pay for the data that adverts consume, and some adverts slow devices or contain harmful software.

However, advertising revenue keeps many websites free, and some adverts are useful. Newspapers, video platforms and search engines depend on it, and without it, readers might have to pay for subscriptions that many cannot afford. A shopper who receives an advert for a product she was looking for may actually benefit. The answer is therefore not to abolish online advertising but to make it less intrusive. Better rules and tools balance both sides: laws should require clear consent before data are collected, limit tracking, and ban the most annoying formats, while browsers and ad blockers allow users to protect themselves. Responsible advertisers who respect users can build trust.

In conclusion, I agree that online advertising is intrusive, but with proper regulation it can remain a fair way to fund content.

237.text:
Some countries fund television and radio channels through licence fees or taxes, and this essay will discuss the benefits for a country that focuses on public broadcasting, using examples from several nations.

To begin with, public broadcasting provides reliable information and cultural programmes that commercial channels may not. Funded by licence fees or taxes, it can serve minorities, schools and remote regions and keep news independent of advertisers. The British Broadcasting Corporation, for example, produces news, drama, children's programmes and educational series that are available to everyone, and its reports are widely trusted around the world. Because public channels do not depend on audience ratings alone, they can broadcast documentaries, classical music and regional languages that attract smaller audiences but add to national culture. In emergencies such as floods, they provide accurate and calm warnings and advice to the whole population.

Furthermore, public broadcasting benefits democracy and society. It offers balanced coverage of elections and political debates, which helps citizens to make informed decisions, and it brings people together through shared experiences such as sporting events and national celebrations. Schools use its programmes in lessons, and its children's channels are free of advertising. The disadvantages are the cost to taxpayers and the risk of political pressure, but strong independence rules, transparent funding and an independent board can protect against these problems. Citizens are better informed and more united in countries with strong public broadcasters, and commercial channels also gain by competing against high standards.

In conclusion, a country that focuses on public broadcasting benefits from independent information, rich culture and a more informed society.

244.text:
When a famous actor smiles from a billboard while holding a perfume bottle or a bank card, viewers may assume that the star really uses it, and many feel that celebrity endorsements are misleading. I agree to a large extent, since stars are paid to praise products they may not use, although some endorsements are genuine.

To begin with, celebrity endorsements can mislead because stars are paid to praise products they may not use. Fans trust the personality and assume that the recommendation is genuine, so claims about health or beauty may influence them without evidence. A footballer who promotes an energy drink, for example, probably does not consume it before matches, and a singer who recommends a face cream may use very different products at home. Contracts often specify what the star must say, and scripts are written by advertising agencies. Some celebrities promote financial products or supplements without understanding them, and followers have lost money or suffered health problems after trusting these messages.

Furthermore, endorsements exploit emotion and not reason. The product becomes attractive because of the fame of the person, not because of its quality, and this encourages purchases that people might otherwise avoid. However, not every endorsement is dishonest. Some stars choose brands that match their values and use them in real life, and a few donate their fees to charity. Transparency rules protect consumers. Laws should require stars to declare clearly when they are paid, ban claims that cannot be proved and punish false statements, and regulators can fine those who break the rules. Viewers should also remember that advertising aims to sell, and they should compare products independently.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that celebrity endorsements are misleading, but stricter transparency can reduce the problem.

Khai thác cảm xúc không lý trí: sản phẩm hấp dẫn nhờ người nổi tiếng không phải chất lượng; nhưng không phải đều thiếu trung thực: chọn thương hiệu hợp giá trị, quyên phí từ thiện; luật yêu cầu công khai được trả, cấm tuyên bố không chứng minh, phạt; người xem so sánh độc lập.
Largely agree; minh bạch giảm vấn đề.
